blocks.text: Carboxylic acids are considerably more acidic than phenols and phenols are even more acidic than alcohols. The relative values of acidity constant or ionization constant, Ka, are given below (table) for a carboxylic acid, phenol or an alcohol.
The acidic strength i.e, extent of ionization of an acid depends upon the stability of its conjugate base. For example,

blocks.alt: Ethanoic acid, CH3-C(=O)-O-H, with -delta on the O and +delta on the H, in equilibrium (H2O over the arrows) with the ethanoate ion, CH3-C(=O)-O-, + H+. Ka = 1.8 x 10^-5; pKa = 4.76.
blocks.caption: Ionisation of ethanoic acid (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 112).

blocks.title: pKa=-log Ka
blocks.text: Higher the Ka or lower the pKa, stronger will be the acid and vice versa.

In the ethanoate ion (the conjugate base), the intensity of the negative charge on oxygen atom is decreased due to delocalization of electrons around the –COOH group. Due to this, the ethanoate ion becomes stabilized thus making it less likely to accept H⁺ ions to form undissociated acid molecule.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The ethanoate ion has no –COOH group: its electrons are delocalised over the –COO⁻ group, that is, over the carbon and both oxygen atoms.

blocks.alt: Two resonance structures of the ethanoate ion joined by a double-headed arrow: CH3-C(=O)-O- and CH3-C(-O-)=O. Curly arrows show the C=O pi electrons moving onto one oxygen and a lone pair of the O- moving back into the C-O bond.
blocks.caption: Delocalisation of the negative charge in the ethanoate ion (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 112).

blocks.text: The presence of an electron donating group (+I effect) will tend to destabilize the carboxylate ion by intensifying the negative charge and thus decreases the acidity of the acid. On the other hand, an electron withdrawing group (-I effect) will tend to stabilize the carboxylate ion by dispersing its negative charge and thus increases the acidity of the acid. For example, methanoic acid is 10 times stronger acid than ethanoic acid.

blocks.alt: H-COOH with the H boxed in yellow and an arrow down to '(-I effect)'; Ka = 1.8 x 10^-4, pKa = 3.75. CH3-COOH with the CH3 boxed and an arrow down to '(+I effect)'; Ka = 1.8 x 10^-5, pKa = 4.75.
blocks.caption: Methanoic acid and ethanoic acid compared (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 112).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed labels read '(-1 effect)' and '(+1 effect)'; the symbol is the letter I (inductive effect): –I and +I.

For example, chloroacetic acid (ClCH₂-COOH) has a pKa of 2.86, indicating that it is a stronger acid than ethanoic acid (pKa = 4.74). Dichloroethanoic acid (Cl₂CH-COOH) is stronger, with a pKa of 1.26. Trichloroacetic acid (Cl₃C-COOH) has a pKa of 0.64, comparable in strength to some mineral acids.

blocks.alt: Displayed formulas of acetic acid (pKa = 4.74), chloroacetic acid (2.86), dichloroacetic acid (1.26) and trichloroacetic acid (0.64): one, two and three H atoms on the CH3 carbon are replaced by Cl. A pink block arrow pointing right is labelled 'Stronger acid'.
blocks.caption: Acetic acid and its chloro-substituted acids (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 112).

blocks.title: Quick Check 23.4
blocks.text:
a) Methanoic acid is stronger than ethanoic acid. Give reason.
b) Place the following acids in order of strength, starting with the strongest acid first.
i) CH₃CH₂COOH
ii) CH₃CCl₂COOH
iii) CH₃CHClCOOH
c) Explain why ethanoic acid is a stronger acid than ethanol.
